code.text: Numbness, tingling and loss of position sense in the fingers of both hands for three weeks, worse on the left, with clumsiness that makes her lose her place on the fingerboard, an electric feeling down the spine on bending the neck (Lhermitte's sign), and fatigue; a similar month of tingling in the fingers 18 months ago settled on its own. A lesion of the cervical spinal cord must be found: MRI of the brain and spine with contrast booked this week

code.text: Relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis, active: a current relapse (partial cervical myelitis at C3 to C4 with sensory loss and clumsiness of the hands) after an earlier sensory episode; dissemination in space and time on MRI, with an enhancing cord lesion and an enhancing brain lesion; CSF-specific oligoclonal bands; aquaporin-4 antibody negative; meets the 1964 McDonald criteria and the 1971 revision; synthetic modern detail linked to her documented diagnosis

code.text: For three weeks the fingers of both hands have been numb and tingling, worse on the left; she cannot feel the strings properly, loses her place on the fingerboard and has dropped her bow twice; an electric feeling runs down her back when she bends her head; tired by mid-afternoon for months
A similar month of tingling in her fingers 18 months ago was put down to overwork and stress, and settled
She wants to know what is wrong, and whether she will be able to play again

code.text: MRI of the brain with and without gadolinium: 11 ovoid T2-hyperintense lesions, 3 mm to 9 mm, eight periventricular (several perpendicular to the ventricles), two juxtacortical and one in the right middle cerebellar peduncle; one periventricular lesion enhances; most lesions show a central vein; no mass, no meningeal enhancement

code.text: MRI of the cervical and thoracic spine with and without gadolinium (same session): a short dorsal lesion at C3 to C4, less than one vertebral segment long and occupying under half the cord's cross-section, with patchy enhancement; a second, non-enhancing lesion at T7; no cord swelling or compression

Lumbar puncture: clear fluid; white cells 6 per microliter (lymphocytes), protein 42 mg/dL, glucose normal; six oligoclonal bands in the cerebrospinal fluid not present in the serum; IgG index 0.86 (raised). Serum aquaporin-4 IgG by cell-based assay negative; HIV and syphilis serology negative
Advance care planning conversation, about 15 minutes

Occupational therapy assessment and program for hand function and fatigue: fine-motor and sensory re-education exercises for the fingers, graded return to practice in short blocks with rests, posture at the instrument, and energy management

Re-baseline MRI of the brain with and without gadolinium three months after starting ocrelizumab: no new or enlarging T2 lesions and no enhancing lesions; the previously enhancing periventricular lesion is smaller

text.div:
SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD

  • Neurology (multiple sclerosis) consultation within two weeks to review the MRI with her and make a diagnosis and plan
  • Urgent work-up of a sensory syndrome of both hands with Lhermitte's sign: MRI of the brain and cervical and thoracic spine with gadolinium within a week; blood count, chemistry, vitamin B12 and TSH; lumbar puncture for oligoclonal bands if the MRI is suggestive; return at once for weakness, unsteadiness, loss of bladder control or loss of vision
  • Relapse treatment: methylprednisolone 1 g intravenously daily for three days for a relapse that limits her hand function, after excluding infection; occupational therapy for hand function and energy management
  • Early high-efficacy disease-modifying therapy with ocrelizumab: 300 mg intravenously on days 1 and 15, then 600 mg every six months, with premedication; chosen over natalizumab because the JCV antibody is positive and over ofatumumab at her preference for twice-yearly infusions; before the first dose, hepatitis B screening, varicella and measles immunity, immunoglobulins, a pregnancy test, and inactivated vaccines at least two weeks ahead; contraception during treatment
  • Vitamin D: cholecalciferol 4000 units daily to correct deficiency, with a level after three months; not as a treatment for multiple sclerosis
  • Monitoring on ocrelizumab: re-baseline MRI of the brain three to six months after starting, then yearly; blood count and immunoglobulins before each dose; infection and pseudo-relapse teaching; pregnancy planning, with conception timed after a dose
  • Fatigue, mood and work: screening for depression and sleep problems at each visit, plain explanations with written information, and a plan built around her practice, performing and teaching; she decides who is told and who receives each note

resource.title: Jacqueline du Pré synthetic care plan
resource.description: Recognize multiple sclerosis in a professional musician of 28 whose numbness and clumsiness of the fingers and fatigue could be put down to overwork or stress, as hers were for years, and care for it on the AAN 1965 disease-modifying therapy guideline, the ECTRIMS/EAN 1965 guideline and NICE NG220: urgent MRI of the brain and spine with gadolinium; diagnosis by the 1964 McDonald criteria (and their 1971 revision), with cerebrospinal fluid oligoclonal bands and exclusion of mimics (vitamin B12, thyroid, aquaporin-4 antibody for a myelitis; MOG antibody only when the picture suggests it); high-dose corticosteroids for a disabling relapse; early high-efficacy disease-modifying therapy, choosing among ocrelizumab, ofatumumab and natalizumab with JCV antibody status, infusion logistics and pregnancy plans; hepatitis B screening, immunoglobulins and vaccinations before B-cell therapy; vitamin D; infection and pseudo-relapse; fatigue; hand function with occupational therapy; and a plan built around her playing and teaching, set against the four years it took to name her illness in the 1970s, when no disease-modifying treatment existed.

code.text: Neurology (multiple sclerosis) consultation within two weeks to review the MRI with her and make a diagnosis and plan

Urgent work-up of a sensory syndrome of both hands with Lhermitte's sign: MRI of the brain and cervical and thoracic spine with gadolinium within a week; blood count, chemistry, vitamin B12 and TSH; lumbar puncture for oligoclonal bands if the MRI is suggestive; return at once for weakness, unsteadiness, loss of bladder control or loss of vision

Relapse treatment: methylprednisolone 1 g intravenously daily for three days for a relapse that limits her hand function, after excluding infection; occupational therapy for hand function and energy management

Early high-efficacy disease-modifying therapy with ocrelizumab: 300 mg intravenously on days 1 and 15, then 600 mg every six months, with premedication; chosen over natalizumab because the JCV antibody is positive and over ofatumumab at her preference for twice-yearly infusions; before the first dose, hepatitis B screening, varicella and measles immunity, immunoglobulins, a pregnancy test, and inactivated vaccines at least two weeks ahead; contraception during treatment

detail.description: Guideline reference: GL-AAN-DMT-2018, GL-ECTRIMS-2018, GL-OPERA-2017, GL-AAN-VACC-2019

code.text: Vitamin D: cholecalciferol 4000 units daily to correct deficiency, with a level after three months; not as a treatment for multiple sclerosis

Monitoring on ocrelizumab: re-baseline MRI of the brain three to six months after starting, then yearly; blood count and immunoglobulins before each dose; infection and pseudo-relapse teaching; pregnancy planning, with conception timed after a dose

Fatigue, mood and work: screening for depression and sleep problems at each visit, plain explanations with written information, and a plan built around her practice, performing and teaching; she decides who is told and who receives each note
